column4: ch-002 chunk 1 (Diop, physical anthropology and images)
column5: Diop opens by arguing humankind began around the great lakes (citing Leakey 1971), so the earliest people were 'negroid', and that Egypt was peopled along the Nile; the chapter text is Diop's own paper, followed (in later chunks) by the symposium record. Chunk 1 says skull studies (Fawcett, Thomson and Randall MacIver, Falkenburger) give mixed results (Falkenburger's predynastic sample: 36% negroid, 33% Mediterranean, 11% Cro-Magnoid, 20% intermediate), and Diop reads those as proving a black basis; Diop also cites Petrie's reading of images (Tera Neter, Narmer, Zoser, Cheops 'Cameroon type', Mentuhotep 'very black') as showing negroid pharaohs and Indo-European captives. Present as Diop's argument [CONTESTED]; the percentages are real data points from his sources but his reading of them is his own.

column4: ch-002 chunk 2 (Diop, melanin, bones, blood, classical authors)
column5: Diop: melanin microscopy of mummy skin from the Marietta excavation (his own samples; no figures are given in the chapter), the Lepsius canon, blood group B in Upper Egypt, classical authors (Herodotus on Colchians 'black skins and kinky hair', Aristotle, Strabo, Diodorus, Ammianus), Volney 1787, and the claim that Egyptian 'kmt' means 'the negroes'. The chapter gives no melanin results for readers to check; blood-group and bone claims are asserted. Herodotus himself writes 'this proves nothing' about colour (quoted by Diop). Course: show Diop's case as presented, with these gaps flagged, and wait for the symposium record for replies [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-002 chunk 3 (Diop, kmt, divine epithets, Wolof comparisons)
column5: Diop: kmt as 'the black men' (he admits Egyptologists read 'kmt' as 'black earth/black country', after the colour of the silt, and says that cannot apply to the plural nisba kmtjw); divine epithets 'black' vs 'red'; Genesis lists Mizraim among Ham's sons; circumcision and totemism; and a Wolof-Egyptian verb and demonstrative comparison (kef, feh, mer/mar) claimed as genetic kinship. The Wolof tables are a sketch, not a full proof, and later publications ask for fuller reconstruction; Diop himself claims he picked 'the least debatable facts'. The Editor's Note (Gamal Mokhtar) states plainly that 'the arguments put forward in this chapter have not been accepted by all the experts'; the chapter closes with Diop's account of the 1974 Cairo symposium. Course: Diop's linguistics = a hypothesis in progress [CONTESTED], not settled.

column4: ch-002 chunk 3 (Diop's account of Cairo 1974 symposium)
column5: Diop quotes the symposium report for agreement points: Vercoutter said percentages for 'blacks, whites and half-castes' cannot be estimated and Egypt was African in writing, culture and thinking; Sauneron said Egyptian cannot be explained as Semitic (Semitic roots a few hundred of several thousand words) and that a genetic link to African languages 'could not be fortuitous'; the report also says there was a 'real lack of balance in the discussions' because not all participants prepared comparable papers. Diop's own later paragraphs (on sickle-cell, Grimaldi 'negroids', Cro-Magnon about 2000 BCE) are his claims, not the symposium's. Compare these with the symposium record in the next chunks before use [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-002 chunk 4 (Cairo 1974: Vercoutter, Leclant, Abdalla replies)
column5: The symposium record opens with Vercoutter: physical anthropology gives 'relatively little reliable data except in Nubia', craniometry is 'generally agreed' not to meet the need, Delta predynastic and pre-Neolithic Upper Egypt are unstudied, and there is no evidence to say the northern and southern Egyptians differed; he frames the two extreme views as 'white' Egyptians with dark pigment versus black Africans throughout. Seve-Soderbergh (Scandinavian Nubia work: 7,000 rock pictures, 1,546 skeletons) says a racial-distinction study of Egypt's peopling is impossible and techno-complexes show Egypt was African. Leclant: Egyptian civilisation African in character but 'race' and culture must be separated; Lepsius, Petrie, Elliot Smith and Derry are 'totally outmoded'; Egyptians called themselves rmt 'men'; Sakkara prisoner statues and sandal stereotypes show northerners (whites) and southerners (negroes) as foreigners. Abdalla: kem does not mean 'black', Egyptian belongs to a proto-Semitic group, Diop's Wolof examples 'neither convincing nor conclusive', Napata people look different from Egyptians. Diop's chapter used Lepsius and Petrie as authorities that Leclant calls outdated [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-002 chunk 5 (Sauneron on kmt; Obenga on Wolof; discussion)
column5: Sauneron at Cairo: kmt/kem means 'black', but the plural nisba kmtyw means only 'those of Kmt' (the black country), like Frank-France-French, not 'black people'; the Egyptians never used it for the black peoples of the hinterland and generally did not use colour words to tell peoples apart. This answers Diop's central philological claim (kmtjw = 'the negroes'). Obenga: argues a genetic link between Egyptian and Wolof/Bantu from morphology (suffix -t, plurals), but Abdalla and others said the similarities could be chance; the report notes Obenga's text is in the final report's Annex II. Gordon-Jaquet: toponymy shows no mass migration since Neolithic times. Devisse: Byzantine manuscripts (6th-12th century) draw some Egyptians as black, a 'northerner's view' inconsistent with the 'white-skinned' theory. Discussion: Diop argues the whole population was black until the Persian occupation; no participant explicitly supported the old 'dark white' theory but 'a number of objections' showed deep disagreement, with one rejecting Diop wholly; Abu Bakr and El Nadury argued mixed population from the Neolithic with Saharan and Semitic inflow (Merimde, first-dynasty fortifications at Abydos), Leclant says the unity was cultural not racial and the Egyptians were 'neither white nor negro' [CONTESTED].

column4: ch-002 chunk 6 (Cairo 1974: where they agreed and where they did not)
column5: The rapporteur's own summary: participants gave 'almost unanimous agreement' only on two working points: (1) the Nile-valley population was most affected by large movements in the Neolithic (migrants from the Eastern Sahara, Diop's rival being movement from the south), and (2) from protodynastic times it was very stable, with high cultural stability. On Diop's 'homogeneous black until the Persian invasion' against a mixed-population view there was 'total disagreement'. Other points: no one was able to date the Saharan inflows; a 500-year gap in Nubia (about 2800-2300 BCE) and none in Lower Nubia about 1000 BCE to the first century CE limit what can be said; the Delta (Merimde, El Omari, Maadi) differs from Upper Egypt and is poorly known; Vercoutter and Leclant note a new type of black representation from the 18th dynasty (tombs of Houy and Rekhmire); the Unesco representative said the terms negro/black/negroid had to be defined, and some experts wanted them avoided. The rapporteur also remarks that Obenga treats a homogeneous culture as implying a homogeneous ethnic base, which he says confused the debate [CONTESTED].

Sauneron's sampling objection: several hundred million people lived in the valley, a few hundred sites and about 2,000 bodies studied, so 'ambitious general conclusions' are 'totally unrealistic'; Vercoutter called the Narmer image enlarged and distorted (Seve-Soderbergh: it could be a Laplander); Vercoutter conceded black people appear in Old Kingdom sculpture but not as the whole population, and asked why Egyptians painted themselves red rather than black (Diop: the red marks the black Egyptian race, women's yellow shows women's paler hue); 'nothing was conceded by either side'. Linguistics: 'large measure of agreement' that Egyptian cannot be explained as Semitic alone and might be related to African languages, but the kmtyw reading as 'Egyptians' (nisba of Kmt 'black land') was affirmed by Sauneron and Abdalla; Sauneron says a 5,000-year gap needs a method (reconstruct a palaeo-African language first); the final recommendations ask for a Unesco inquiry into racial standards, re-study of skeletal and skin remains, Delta archaeology and linguistic study of Kaw-Kaw. Meroitic: script read but language not understood (13,405 recorded word units) [CONTESTED].

The close of the annex: Diop proposes comparing Meroitic with 100 African languages (500-word lists on punched cards, computer matching) as a method of decipherment, Leclant endorses it as a research procedure, Sauneron wants a sound method first; recommendations: finish the Meroitic corpus and vocabulary (Repertoire d'Epigraphie Meroitique), train Sudanese linguists, survey languages like Kaw-Kaw. Meroitic remains unread as a language in 1974-84 (script deciphered, language not). Module 2: say so; never claim Meroitic has been 'translated' [FIRM that it is not understood].

column4: ch-011 chunk 1 (Leclant, Kush and the 25th dynasty)
column5: Leclant: the Kushite 25th dynasty 'sprang from the soil' (not Egyptian refugees or Libyans), el-Kurru tombs from the late 9th century BCE; Kashta around 750 BCE in Upper Egypt; Peye's Victory stele (159 lines) against the Libyan princes; Shabaka about 713; Taharqa 690-664 resisted Assyria (Bible mentions), Ashurbanipal sacked Thebes 663 BCE; Psamtek II's expedition of 591 BCE took Napata and moved the capital to Meroe, 'one of the few really secure synchronisms'; Napata stayed the religious centre, kings buried at Nuri until the end of the 4th century BCE; the first capital transfer is attributed by Leclant to the Egyptian raid, 'long underestimated'. Confirms the course's Kush outline; use his chronology as the working one [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-011 chunk 2 (Meroe: capital, queens, writing, fall)
column5: Leclant gives climate and economy, not only the Egyptian raid, as reasons for moving to Meroe (wider steppe, summer rain, hafirs, fuel for iron) but says calling Meroe 'the Birmingham of Africa' is 'exaggerated' (Trigger, Amborn); Meroitic chronology rests on Reisner's king list, 'chancy results' revised since; Diodorus's priests-force-the-king-to-suicide story has 'no corroboration'; the Meroitic script (23 signs, Griffith's 1909 key) can be read but the language 'whose nature is still not known' and the 800-odd texts cannot be translated; Candaces Amanirenas and Amanishakheto, war with Rome and the 21-20 BCE treaty of Samos, Meroe's last dated reign Teqorideamani (253 CE); Meroe fell probably to the Noba (not just Aksum), Ezana of Aksum boasts of a campaign against 'the Nubas' about 330 CE; the chapter says the idea that Meroe spread ironworking across Africa rests on 'it would seem' only, and the Kushite-flight-to-Darfur idea is 'pure hypothesis'. Module 2: the Meroe iron-spread claim should be called hypothesis [CONTESTED], and 'Birmingham of Africa' removed or flagged.

After Meroe, Lower Nubia's Group X or Ballana culture (4th to mid-6th century) with rich tumuli at Ballana and Qustul (excavated 1931-3); the Blemmyes (Beja nomads) and Nobades (Noba) are 'barely more than names'; Philae's Isis temple stayed open until Justinian closed it (535-7); the Monophysite missionary Julian converted the Nobadian king (543) per John of Ephesus, Longinos converted the Noba about 570, King Silko boasted of beating the Blemmyes in an undated Greek inscription at Kalabsha. Module 2: connects Kush to Christian Nubia; dates [PROBABLE].

Hakem (with Hrbek and Vercoutter): Napatan dynasty of local origin (Libyan or Theban-priest theories 'weak'), king chosen from the royal brethren by army chiefs, officials and clan heads with oracular confirmation 'merely a formal ratification' (Diodorus saw only the ceremony); fourteen of 27 kings before Nastasen were brothers of earlier kings; descent through female line; Reisner's two parallel Napatan kingdoms abandoned by most scholars; Diodorus and Strabo's priestly order for royal suicide persisted till Ergamenos about 250-125 BCE per those authors (Leclant earlier said 'no corroboration'), so say it is reported by Greek writers, not confirmed [CONTESTED]; the candace title (Kdke) first meant queen-mother, the first reigning queen is Shanakdakhete in the early second century BCE; only four reigning queens known to have used qere (Amanirenas, Amanishakheto, Nawidemak, Maleqereabar). Module 2.

Kush was 'not a centralised state': a king with palace officials, a Lower Nubian Paqar/peshte administration after the Roman conquest of Egypt, vassal princedoms (Pliny's 45 kings in the island of Meroe), and nomad groups raided for cattle and slaves; Meroe was the royal residence by the evidence of infant court burials; economy rested on cattle-breeding above all (wealth, offerings, metaphors), irrigation by shaduf then the saqiya (Dakka and Gammai sites, third century BCE), sorghum, cotton (textile export), vines and dates; Lower Nubia was depopulated in the early Napatan period until the saqiya; camels came at the end of the first century BCE; Hakem argues overgrazing and desiccation helped cause Meroe's decline from the first century CE, and that cotton plantations were destroyed by Ezana. Module 2: say the Meroe decline had several causes (climate, grazing, Noba, Aksum) [PROBABLE].

Hakem lays out the iron dispute: Sayce's 1911 'Birmingham of ancient Africa' was long accepted; Wainwright, Arkell, Shinnie, Trigger, Tylecote and Amborn objected (few iron objects in graves, bronze outnumbers iron even late, Amborn thought the slag heaps were other industries and that iron was imported), but a 1977 Toronto paper by Shinnie and Kense says iron-smelting furnaces were found at Meroe (Begrawiya); Tylecote reports smelting traces before 200 BCE; he calls the question 'far from concluded'. Gold: Kush produced about 1,600,000 kg over antiquity (Quiring's computation, treat as an estimate [THIN EVIDENCE]), Taharqa endowed a temple with 110 kg in nine years, Nastasen exacted nearly 300 kg; silver and copper imported; two pottery traditions (hand-made by women, wheel-made by men). Module 2: replace 'Meroe spread iron' with 'iron smelting at Meroe is attested but its scale and role in spreading ironworking are disputed' [CONTESTED].

Hakem: Meroe's trade peaked in Ptolemaic times, turned to the Red Sea in the early first century BCE as Aksum rose, and collapsed in the third-century Roman crisis; slavery was mainly domestic (more women than men named), exports of black slaves to Egypt in Roman times, 'never the main base of production'; social structure 'almost impossible' to describe (only rulers, aristocracy, priests, slaves and a probable middle class); religion: one religion with Amun temples and about 32 recorded lion temples (Apedemak, Sebiumeker), so 'two types of temple, one religion'; Amun's priests lost control after Ergamenes; the Meroe Amun temple dates to the end of the first century BCE. Module 2.

column4: ch-015 chunk 1 (Anfray, Aksum sources and sites)
column5: Anfray: Aksum's history is known mostly from coins, Ezana/Kaleb inscriptions and archaeology, with 'patchy' knowledge and little dated except inscriptions; earliest king recorded is Zoscales (Greek text, end of the first century CE), 'tradition is unfortunately very unreliable' for the king lists; the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (about the end of the first century) names Aksum and Adulis; earliest Ethiopic script inscriptions are second-century, derived from south Arabian forms (earlier pseudo-Sabaean inscriptions belong to the later first millennium BCE); a text attributed to Mani calls Aksum 'the third kingdom in the world' (third century); about forty major sites; Dongour castle (seventh century), Kaleb and Gebre Meskel tombs (crypts probably older, reused 7th-8th century), Matara villas and churches, Adulis basilicas (the 'palace' reads as a church). Module 2.

Aksum: planned towns without walls, Adulis and Matara as market towns, architecture of stone, tiered podiums, projecting/recessed walls and clay mortar; the giant stelae (one about 33 m, nine storeys carved) are 'funerary cippi' of uncertain meaning, the 17 m slab and 27 throne bases enigmatic, one stele was taken to Rome in 1937 (Anfray says erected near Caracalla theatre; it is the course's well-known restitution story); Matara and Anza stelae of the third or early fourth century carry the crescent and Ge'ez; coins give 18 kings' names, bronze, no dates, earliest Endybis in the third century, Greek legends first, Ge'ez from Wazeba, cross after Ezana's conversion; Ethiopic script from the second century derived from south Arabian, Ge'ez syllabic from Ezana; imported Mediterranean amphoras, Indian-Ocean glass; 'imaginary architecture' of the stelae has no known parallel. Module 2.

Anfray: Aksum grew from a pre-Aksumite (south Arabian-influenced, 5th-4th century BCE) northern-plateau culture with continuity of sites, the swing plough, the god Astar and architecture, but a break around the first centuries CE: new triad Mahrem, Beher, Meder in Ezana's texts, new pottery, Aksum itself with no appreciable past before the first century; trade: Red Sea growth in the first two centuries (Hippalus, 120 ships a year from Myos Hormos in Augustus's time per Strabo), ivory the main export; the Bible translated into Ge'ez about the fifth century; Anfray concludes that Aksum owes its qualities 'to its African roots'. The chapter keeps the earlier south Arabian influence while arguing the civilisation is African; Module 2: say Aksum is a local Ethiopian-plateau civilisation with Sabaean-derived script, not a colony of Arabia [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-016 chunk 1 (Kobishanov, Aksum power and trade)
column5: Kobishanov: Aksum appears in Ptolemy's time as a 'young' kingdom (the Periplus's Zoscales), balanced by Meroe; Aksumite kings Gadara and son led anti-Sabaean wars in south Arabia between 183 and 213 and 'Azbah about 300; Mani's Kephalaia (216-76) calls Aksum one of the four greatest empires; the state was a king of kings with vassal negus (Beja kings ruling about 1,100 subjects), administration 'poorly developed', relatives in command; Aksum was the first tropical African state to mint coin (Endybis, second half of the third century), gold/silver/copper, Byzantine-like; exports mostly hunted or collected goods (ivory, rhino horn, obsidian, tortoise shell, gold dust, slaves), imports wine, oil, cloth, Indian iron and steel; Cosmas's gold-for-meat story likely a fable. Module 2: say 'first tropical African state to mint its own coins (third century CE) per this chapter' [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-016 chunk 2 (Aksum trade control and culture)
column5: Kobishanov: Aksum's wealth came from controlling Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb routes and royal control of ivory, gold and slaves; Cosmas describes a secret royal caravan of up to 500 to Sasu (south-west Ethiopia) for gold; 'Martyrdom of Aretha' lists ships at Gabaza in 525 (9 Indian, 7 Farasan, 15 Elat, 22 Egyptian, 7 Iotaba); Ezana's records give about 32,500 cattle and 51,000 sheep as spoils and 25,000 cattle to Beja groups (his own figures, [TRADITIONAL DATE]-type royal boasts); stelae 33.5 m, monolith 17.3 m, 'unparalleled in tropical Africa' (chapter claim); pagan religion close to ancient south Arabia (Astar, Behér, Meder, Hawbas) and the Ge'ez word for God Egziabher comes from Behér. Kobishanov reads Aksum as an 'early feudal empire' (Soviet framework), which is his model not the evidence. Module 2.

Aksum's religion resembled ancient south Arabia (Astar, Behér, Meder, Mahrem as war god translated Ares in Greek texts), ancestor cult at stelae (hawelt), and travellers' gods (Almaqah, Hathor/Ptah finds, small Buddha images); 'indefinite monotheism' in Ezana's Nubian inscription bridged to Christianity; Greek was a state language (Frumentius, Ezana's tutor, became the first bishop); vocalised Ethiopic script reflects Ge'ez phonology and could only have been made by an Ethiopian, but the idea of marking vowels shows Indian (Brahmi) parallels per Grohmann; the script then influenced Armenian (Olderogge's suggestion, a hypothesis). Module 2: the Ge'ez syllabary is a local innovation on a Sabaean base, with the Indian-parallel idea only 'quite probable' [PROBABLE].

column4: ch-027 chunk 1 (Andah, West African food production)
column5: Andah (1981): the evidence 'does not support' the belief that outside (Saharan or Near Eastern) influence mainly produced West African food production or metalworking; cultigens indigenous (millet, fonio, African rice, cowpea, Guinea yams, oil palm); domesticated shorthorn cattle at Uan Muhuggiag (Libya) from about 5590 BCE and Adrar Bous (Air) about 3830-3790 BCE, about 1,200 years before the Nile Valley, so not from Egypt; Amekni (Hoggar) pollen of possibly domesticated Pennisetum dated 6100-4850 BCE is a hint, not proof; the inland Niger delta and Futa Jallon fringe may be nuclear areas for rice and millets; Tichitt-Walata 8-phase sequence with incipient Cenchrus and Pennisetum cultivation about 1500-1100 BCE (Munson's reading criticised by Andah as under-reading earlier cultivation). Module 1: use 'independent West African origin of cereal cultivation, with Saharan pastoralism earlier than the Nile' as an evidence-based line; note the 'plant evidence is thin' [PROBABLE].

Andah: two nuclear areas in West Africa (Sahel/Sudanic seed crops, forest-fringe roots and oil palm), with African rice possibly domesticated about 3,500 years ago in the inland Niger delta (Porteres) and spread down the Gambia and Casamance; Iwo Eleru shows the Neolithic change just after 4000 BCE (3620 BCE) and Ukpa 2935+-140 BCE; the 'Guinea Neolithic' came earlier in the forest fringe and 'was independent of northern influences'; Daima mound (Lake Chad) shows herders by the early 6th century BCE, Connah rejects using oral tradition to name Sao 2,500 years back; Kintampo-Ntereso (Ghana) shows food production by 1300-1400 BCE; sorghum: Stemler et al. suggest the Caudatum race arose after about 350 CE in the Sudan. Mixed claims here: radiocarbon dates quoted are older (uncalibrated?) and the chapter does not say whether dates are calibrated, so give them as approximate [PROBABLE]. Module 1 and 5.

column4: ch-027 chunk 3 (Andah, early iron and copper in West Africa)
column5: Andah: Nok people were working iron 'by 500 BCE and probably some time before' (still using stone tools too), terracotta figurines, influence 'far reaching' (Willett on links to Ife art: 'difficult not to believe'); Daima iron from the fifth/sixth century CE; Sao sites dates 425 BCE to 1700 CE are 'not satisfactorily defined' (Shaw); Akjoujt (Mauritania) copper smelting dated 570-400 BCE with about 40 tons extracted, early trans-Saharan copper trade possible; Igbo-Ukwu iron at least by the 9th century CE; Ife dated thirteenth-fourteenth century by present evidence, Willett thinks it may reach back to about the sixth century CE (a speculative line [THIN EVIDENCE]); Kouga tumulus dated 950 BCE +-120 (as printed; calibration unknown); middle Niger and Senegambia mounds and burial tumuli mostly uninvestigated and looted. The chapter says iron working probably began in West Africa 'at both ends of the Sahel/savannah zone', indigenous. Module 1 and 5: place Nok iron before 500 BCE as the firm minimum; keep Ife 6th-century idea as speculation.

The volume's own introduction says the history from about 7000 BC to AD 700 still consists largely of suppositions, because firmly dated sources are scarce; suppositions are founded on rare information, not invented. Use as the opening caution of the evidence-kinds lesson.

Egypt has the continent's richest dated sources. The Palermo Stone lists kings to the Fifth Dynasty (about 2450 BC) with year-by-year annals from the Third; the Turin Papyrus gives a king list to about 1200 BC; both are broken. Manetho's history (3rd century BC) survives only in excerpts but gives the thirty-one dynasties. None of these are in the course yet.

Egyptian royal texts were written to show that the Pharaoh kept Ma'at against chaos, so a king list or monument is a statement of royal ideology as well as a record. Use this when a lesson quotes an Egyptian king's own words.

Egypt had written king lists but dated by the reign of the king in office (Year 10 of Pharaoh N), so every date needs a king list and reign lengths. The Turin and Palermo gaps mean a complete list is not certain. Adding all reigns gives over 4000 years, which was accepted until about 1900; parallel dynasties and co-regents overlap, so the total is wrong. Good contrast for the 'written calendar' lesson.

An astronomical anchor fixed Egyptian dates: the heliacal rising of Sothis (Sirius) coincided with the Nile flood, and the Egyptians recorded the drift of their calendar. The adoption of the calendar is now placed at 2785-2782 BC, not 4245-4242 BC. Reigns of Senusret III, Amenhotep I and Thutmose III are fixed to within about four years. The basic chronology starts at about 3000 BC.

The race of the ancient Egyptians was argued from 1874; a 1974 UNESCO symposium in Cairo did not close it. Anthropologists now doubt that physical criteria can name a skeleton's race. The volume's view is that the Nile population was mixed and varied over time. Use this when a lesson on Diop's claims reports the Cairo reply.

The volume explains why Nubia did not take up writing while Egypt did: the Nile valley's dense, irrigated population needed administration and records, while Nubian groups, with more stock-raising and mobility, stayed in oral tradition. This is the volume's interpretation, not proven. Use it in the written-versus-oral lesson as a contested explanation, and say who proposes it.

Egyptian hieroglyphs were built from word-signs, homophones and phonetic complements; the Nile-valley writing system is shown to be African in its signs (Nilotic fauna and flora) and to have formed before the Narmer palette (about 3000 BC). Use as evidence that writing was an African development, not a borrowed one. Hieroglyphs also served the state's accounting and organisation of Nile works.

The terms Upper and Lower Egypt are fallacious for the state's formation period. Upper Egypt in the predynastic period stopped at El Kab in the south and near the Faiyum in the north, with its centre at Naqada and later Abydos; Lower Egypt started at the Faiyum and centred near modern Cairo-Heliopolis. Use this in any lesson on Egypt's unification.

Egyptian history is uneven: strong centralised periods (Old Kingdom about 2700-2200 BC, Middle about 2000-1800, New about 1600-1100) have many sources, while three Intermediate Periods (2200-2000, 1800-1600, 1100-750 BC) have almost none. About a third of Pharaonic time is poorly known. Use as the caveat on any Egypt-based chronology in the course.

Imports into early Egypt (ivory, ebony, incense, obsidian) show contact with peoples further south and so with Africa south of the Sahara. The volume calls the Mesopotamian-invasion theory resting on the flimsiest evidence, and the Delta before dynastic times is virtually unknown. Use when a lesson claims outside invaders or eastern influence on Egypt.

Two Egyptian objects found far south, an Osiris statuette on the Lualaba in Zaire and a Thutmose III cartouche statue south of the Zambezi, were once claimed as proof of contact. A critical study of how they were found does not support that; Arkell's Byzantine Egypt-Ghana link is also weak. Use as the worked example of an object out of context in the evidence-kinds lesson.

Akan links to Egypt: Meyerowitz's vulture symbol and Ptah/Odomankoma parallels are interesting but not conclusive evidence of contact. The serpent cult in many African cultures may come from local observation; one suggestion is India, which the volume does not accept without evidence. Use in the Akan lesson to separate parallel from influence.

From the Old Kingdom the Nubians (Nehesi) were soldiers and labour under Egyptian control; Egypt organised a Governor of the South by the end of the 5th dynasty. Libyans ruled Egypt in the 22nd-23rd dynasties, which provoked Napatan (Kushite) action and set up the Ethiopian dynasty founded by Piankhi (Peye). Use in the Kush lesson as the black-white political rivalry that turned Kush towards Egypt.

Harkhuf's dwarf dancer from Yam is sometimes taken as proof of a Pygmy people on the upper Nile. The volume says this rests on an unsupported assumption; Montet notes that an earlier traveller brought back a dwarf from Punt, so the dwarf's origin is not known. Use as a worked example of a single object carrying a large inference.

Herodotus (IV, 42) says Necho II's Phoenicians sailed round Africa, but the account is contested: the Phoenicians may have been the source, and there is no proof the voyage happened. Use in the written-sources lesson: say who wrote, when, and what each claim rests on, and note that a famous account can be doubted.

Punt was a Red Sea trading partner for incense, ebony and ivory, located by most now on the Horn (Somali coast from Cape Guardafui); expeditions went by sea, shown by inscriptions from Wadi Gasus, and Hatshepsut's voyage is pictured at Deir el-Bahari. Use in the Aksum or Red Sea lesson: the Red Sea route and the Horn trade come before Aksum.

Principle for the evidence lesson: an influence spread over 5000 years is not proof of contact at the same time, and traces of contact are not proof of continuity. Shared features (headrests, sacred kingship, the ram cult, doubles or kas) can arise independently because they are functional. Use as the test for every claimed African-Egyptian link.

The Nok tin hypothesis: a suggestion that Nok's metal came from tin mines at Bauchi and reached the Nile valley is called a mere academic hypothesis; Schaeffer argues the Egyptians' tin came from Syria. Use in the Nok lesson in module 1 as an example of a tempting but unsupported source of a metal.

Akan and other West African doubles (kas), and the Dogon's voodoo pottery, have been compared with Egyptian practice, but the volume says such parallels are not yet evidence of influence and that influence could run the other way. Use in the Akan lesson as a caution against reading Egyptian origin into Akan belief.

Evidence loss: the volume estimates that temples, estates and palaces kept hundreds of kilometres of papyrus registers, yet only a few hundred metres have been rediscovered. Use in the 'evidence kinds and blind spots' lesson: the surviving record is a small and biased sample.

Convergence: glass-making, writing and early metalwork may have been invented independently in Asia and the Nile valley. Attributing an invention to one place without good dating is hazardous, because radiocarbon is too coarse for a century or two. Use in the evidence lesson when a claimed diffusion lacks dates.

Meroe took up glass-making: Meroitic rulers imported Alexandrian glass at first but then adopted its manufacturing techniques and spread them up the Nile valley. Use in the Meroe lesson as a case of an African state taking a technology from Egypt after the Pharaonic period.

Egyptian arithmetic was empirical: multiplication by doubling, fractions with numerator 1, and no zero. Whether Egyptian algebra existed depends on whether algebra without abstract symbols counts. Use in the arithmetic worked example to show that the course's own calculations (our arithmetic) are not Egyptian methods.

Pharaonic building forms reached Africa through the Kushite kingdoms: pyramids, pylons and small well-cut stone masonry are said to have passed to Napata and Meroe. Use in the Kush lesson on the Meroitic pyramids, as an example of an African state adapting an Egyptian form rather than copying it.

The Meroitic language is still not read, so the empire's reach and its effect on other African cultures cannot be judged from its own texts. Use in the Meroe lesson as the limit of what the evidence can show.

Evidence is shaped by when digging happened. No excavations were made before the first Aswan dam (1896), so sites were destroyed before anyone recorded them; excavation became routine only with each raise (1902, 1928-38). Lower Nubia is therefore well known while the Sudan south of the Second Cataract is largely unexcavated. Use as the worked example of a blind spot in the evidence-kinds lesson.

Knowledge of Egypt-Nubia relations after about 2000 BC depends entirely on Egyptian sources, and those tend to record military expeditions. Archaeology in Lower Nubia gives the rest. Use in the written-sources lesson as the case of a source that describes one side only.

The A-Group people of Lower Nubia are no longer thought to have migrated from the north. They descended from local Neolithic groups between the First and Third Cataracts, related to those of the upper valley. Use in the Nubia lesson in place of any north-to-south migration story.

The Nubians were black; Egyptian drawings before about 1580 BC separate the Nehesyu of Lower Nubia from the newcomer Kushites, who had facial traits still seen in Central and West Africa. Use as the chapter's caution: the volume does not join the negro-or-hamitic debate, and the lesson should not either.

column4: ch-009.txt chunk 2 (Ch 8 Adam, with Vercoutter) vs ch-005.txt chunk 2
column5: Pygmies: Adam says the translation deneg = pygmy 'is now broadly accepted', so Old Kingdom Egypt had contact with equatorial forest peoples; Zayed and Devisse (ch-005) say there is no proof the Harkhuf dwarf was a pygmy and that it rests on an unsupported assumption. Show both in the Harkhuf lesson and say the question is open.

Kerma (the kingdom later called Kush) was probably the first African empire known to history; its capital's size and its metallurgy suggest it reached far up the Nile and to the Red Sea. The Hyksos king turned to the Kushite ruler for a joint attack on Thebes (the Kamose episode), showing Kush as a power in its own right. Use in the Kush lesson, with the outlying areas flagged as unexcavated.

Copper was smelted in Africa: an Old Kingdom settlement at Buhen (found 1961-2, fifth dynasty seals) had furnaces for local copper about 2500 BC. The Nubian skill in copper and gold about 500 years later is put down to that early metallurgy. Use in the metallurgy lesson as evidence of African-made metal, not only imports from Sinai.

Cadaverous shepherds painted on Fifth Dynasty tombs (about 2350 BC) are read as drought migrants fleeing the drying Sahara and Sahel. The volume calls this tempting rather than proved. Use with the word tempting in any lesson on climate-driven migration.

Conquest of Nubia took several reigns: Ahmosis to Seti I and Ramses II ran campaign after campaign. Nubians fled south and the number of tombs fell, which forced Pharaohs further south for gold and goods. By Thutmose I the land between the Second and Fourth Cataracts was held. Use in the New Kingdom Nubia lesson.

From Thutmose IV (about 1450 BC) Egyptian tomb images of Africans change to a new physical type resembling Shilluk, Dinka and Kordofan peoples. The volume reads this as expeditions or intermediaries reaching far south, but no survey of those routes has been made. Use as a visual-evidence caution.

The volume warns that the role of the north in African diffusion is exaggerated because so little of the south has been excavated; the theories of diffusion stay theories until the Sudd, Kordofan, Darfur, Chad and the Ethiopian approaches are studied. Use in the method lesson as the reason northern-first explanations need checking.

The B-Group, a supposed separate people of Lower Nubia in the Old Kingdom, is now generally held to be doubtful. Its graves show A-Group features in decline, so they may be impoverished A-Group graves after repeated Egyptian attacks. Use in the Nubia lesson as the current view and the reason, with the older label marked as rejected.

Harkhuf made four journeys to Yam under Merenre and Pepi II. One returned with 300 donkeys loaded with incense, ebony, oil, panther skins, tusks and tree trunks; his peers Pepinakht fought the Wawat and Irtet and brought Nubian chiefs to court. Use in the Nubia lesson to show trade and force in the same records.

The C-Group of Lower Nubia (First Intermediate Period to the 16th century BC) has no agreed origin. Explanations are a continuation of the A-Group, migration from the eastern desert or Atbara, migration from Libya, or cultural evolution; the volume says each remains a hypothesis. Use the same wording in the lesson.

Royal propaganda as evidence: a Leningrad papyrus has a prophecy that a king named Amenys, son of a woman of Ta-Zeti (Nubia), would end the troubles. It was written to make Amenemhet I's accession legitimate, and the volume says he may have had Nubian descent. Use in the written-sources lesson alongside the Ma'at point from the introduction.

Trade rules at the frontier: the stele of Senusret III at Semna forbade Nubians to pass downstream except to trade at Iken (Mirgissa). A Middle Kingdom chain of about seventeen named forts ran from Semna to Shellal; Buhen's fort was 172 by 160 metres with a 6.5-metre ditch. Use in the Nubia lesson on the Middle Kingdom.

Kerma: Reisner's view that Kerma was an Egyptian governors' centre has been largely rejected. Hintze reads the Western Dufufa as a native ruler's residence and the cemetery as Nubian (no mummification, 200 to 300 people buried alive with the owner). The volume says a Middle Kingdom trading post is not ruled out and Dongola is largely unexcavated. Show both readings in the Kerma lesson.

The Kerma tumuli show a Nubian ruling family with human sacrifice on a large scale, and its wares combine native and Egyptian techniques. It is not yet settled whether Egyptian craftsmen made the wares or native makers copied them. Use with the Kerma lesson, and keep 'Kerma was Egyptian' out unless the source supports it.

Egyptianisation worked top-down: chiefs' sons were schooled at the Egyptian court until they forgot their own language, and the Nubian upper class then set the pattern for commoners. Burial moved from the side-lying crouch to extended burial in a coffin. Use as the mechanism of the New Kingdom takeover in the Nubia lesson.

Administration: Nubia was split into Wawat (Nekhen to the Second Cataract) and Kush (Second to Fourth Cataracts), run by a viceroy titled King's son of Kush, who delivered tribute to the vizier at Thebes. Local chiefs kept their districts in return for loyalty. Use as the administrative detail in the New Kingdom lesson.

Violence in the New Kingdom record: Amenophis II's stele says one of seven captured princes was sent to Nubia and hanged on the wall around Napata, 'so that the victorious might of His Majesty be seen for eternity'. Use with the Napata lesson as the Egyptian record of power in the south.

The Nubian dark age: after Heri-Hor's rise (about 1085 BC) Nubia has little recorded history until Kush suddenly emerges as a great power in the eighth century BC. Use as the gap that the Napata lesson has to explain, with the Egyptian sources saying little for those centuries.

Gold drove Nubia's New Kingdom economy: the annual tribute of Wawat was only 550 pounds of gold under Thutmose III (Hintze), and gold came from the Wadi el-Alaki and Wadi Gabgada and the Nile valley mines as far as Abu Hamed. Use in the economy part of the New Kingdom lesson, with the figure attributed.

Nubia's Christianity came before its official conversion (the Byzantine mission of 543 described by John of Ephesus): Christian graves, lamps and pottery with the cross appear in the Nobadian X-Group, and monasteries existed from the late fifth century. Some scholars date the Faras church later. Use in the Nubia lesson with the date disputed.

After the Meroitic kingdom fell, three Christian kingdoms formed (Nobadia, Makuria, Alodia); Makuria took Melkite Christianity from Justinian's mission (567-70), then Monophysite by 660-700, and the united kingdom was made under Merkurios (697). Use in the late Nubia lesson as the state structure after Meroe.

The baqt, a treaty signed after the Arab conquest of Egypt (641), bound Nubia to an annual tribute of slaves and goods and the Arabs to supply food and clothing. It held in principle for seven centuries, with raids between, and trade continued. Use in the trade lesson as an early Nile-Sudan treaty, with the slave tribute stated plainly.

Much of Christian Nubia's chronology comes from Arabic writers (al-Yaqubi, al-Masudi, Maqrizi and others), not from Nubian sources. Use in the written-sources lesson: even an African state's chronology can rest on outside writers, so check each claim against who wrote it.

Language of the record is not the language of the people: at Faras the aristocracy and church spoke Greek and the clergy understood Coptic, but Nubian was spoken widely while its written traces only date from about the mid-ninth century. Use in the written-sources lesson: a silent oral language does not mean an unrecorded society.

Before the Aksumite kingdom (second century BC on Ptolemy's evidence), Greek and Latin writers say almost nothing. The earliest hard mention is Ptolemy II's port of Adulis (mid-third century BC). Pliny mentions elephant hunters in the mountains, but the link of that name to Aksum is conjectural. Use in the Aksum lesson as the start of the written record and the gap before it.

The south Arabian period in northern Ethiopia is dated by palaeography of south Arabian inscriptions to the fifth and fourth centuries BC. The temple at Yeha (about 186 by 15 metres on an eight-tier base) is the only standing monument of that time. Use in the Aksum lesson for the chronology and the one visible building.

The Haoulti naos and seated statues (Tigray, pre-Aksumite) are interpreted in several ways: a cult statue in a processional naos, a queen or dignitary, or a goddess. Parallels run to Marib, Asia Minor and Persepolis. The volume prefers a stone processional naos. Use the statues as contested evidence and say which reading is preferred.

Image evidence is ambiguous: the lozenged hair on the Haoulti statues could be stylised curls or woolly hair, and the same device appears on Persepolis figures. The volume says this does not allow ethnic conclusions. Use in the visual-evidence lesson as a case where the picture cannot settle identity.

The pre-Aksumite rulers were called mukarribs of Saba and of Diamat in south Arabian style, and the Ethiopian dynasts used Sabaean titles. The volume reads the title as a claim of south Arabian descent and political rank, not a territory; their own people may be the ancestors of the Ge'ez speakers. Use in the Aksum lesson on who ruled and what the titles meant.

Dating the south Arabian arrival in Ethiopia: small groups of immigrants may have brought the swing-plough and the first stone villages. The volume calls this possible and not proved, under economic and demographic pressure not yet understood. Use in the Aksum origins lesson, marked as a hypothesis.

Almaqah, the moon god worshipped in south Arabia, is the god of the pre-Aksumite temple at Yeha, of the incense altars and of most dedications at Gobochela, Matara and Addi Galamo, with Athtar (Venus) and two sun goddesses. Use in the religion part of the Aksum lesson, with the Yeha temple as the case.

Label debate: some scholars see a distinctive Ethiopian culture (Pirenne, Anfray) and propose Ethiopo-Sabaean; others stress south Arabian origins (Conti-Rossini). The volume says the apparent superiority of African works may come from the thin research in Yemen. Use in the Aksum lesson to show the debate and say the superiority claim is weak.

Meroe as the driver of metalworking: the intermediary period (about the third century BC on) shows Meroitic bronze bowls and amulets, and the metal and pottery expansion is put down to Meroe, which spread metal techniques across Africa. The decline of Meroe and of south Arabia may have let Ethiopia take control of gold, incense and ivory trade. Use in the Aksum lesson as the reason Aksum rose.

Iron and gold in the pre-Aksumite intermediary period: iron tools (rings, scissors, swords, daggers, sickles) probably began then, bronze was more common, and gold appears as rings and beads. Thick open bronze rings may have served as money, a question the volume leaves open. Use in the metallurgy lesson, with the money question marked as open.

Urbanisation: specialised craftsmen and early towns (Yeha, Melazo, Matara, Adulis) appear by the intermediary period, with sanctuaries at the centre of each settlement. Use in the Aksum origins lesson on towns.

No date for Aksum's conversion is secure. Ethiopian chronicles give 257 (arrival) and 315 (bishop); other dates (333, 343, 350) are called arbitrary. Working from the death of Ella Amida (about 320-35) and the age of majority, the volume puts Ezana's baptism between 350 and 360. Use this as a range, not a year, in the Christian Aksum lesson.

The Philae inscription (in Greek) records the visit in 360 of Abratoeis, an Aksumite Christian viceroy, to the Roman emperor, who received him with full honours. The emperor was probably Constans II, an Arian Christian. This is the earliest dated sign that Aksum's court was Christian, and it also links Aksum to the Arian controversy. Use in the Christian Aksum lesson.

Ezana's first Christian inscription (DAE II) opens 'with the help of the Lord of Heaven and Earth' and avoids naming Christ or the Trinity, which suggests a gradual conversion that fitted Christianity into the old god's place. Use in the conversion lesson as the proof that a king's religion changed by stages.

Source conflict: the local king lists (Tarike Neguest, Guedel Tekle Haymanot) give different names and dates for the same kings from the inscriptions and coins, and Ezana is called pagan by some and believer by others. Use in the written-sources lesson: when chronicle and coin disagree, the coin is the firmer evidence.

Pre-Christian religion: the Aksumite national god Mahrem was equated with Greek and Egyptian gods (Zeus, Amun), while Kushitic groups worshipped natural objects. The volume says Greek-speaking kings allowed such equations. Use in the pre-Christian religion section.

The Nine Saints' arrival: the Tarike Neguest puts them in the reign of Ella Amida, which local sources date to 460-470 or 487-497, so the arrival falls between those dates; a sixth-century arrival under Kaleb and Gebre Meskel is less likely. Use in the lesson on the Nine Saints as a date range, with the Monophysite link explained.

Why Aksum was Monophysite: after Chalcedon (451) Monophysites fled to Egypt and Arabia, and Aksum's bishops came from Alexandria, so Aksum took the Monophysite side. The volume ties this to the later Ethiopian church name Tewahedo. Use in the Christian Aksum and Himyar lessons.

Kaleb's campaign (about 525): the Jewish king Dhu Nuwas massacred the Christians of Najran in 523, and Kaleb landed in Himyar, killed Dhu Nuwas and sacked Zafar and Najran. The volume gives two army sizes, 120,000 men and 60 warships (called inaccurate) and 30,000 men. Use in the Himyar lesson with the figures attributed and the disagreement shown.

Names change by source: Kaleb is Hellesthaios or Elle Atsbaha in Greek sources, Dhu Nuwas is Masruc, Yussuf or Finhas, and Najran's Christians are named after Harite in the Ge'ez text. The volume uses one name and says so. Use in the sources lesson: when a name changes, track the language of the source, and show the variants once.

Language does not give ethnicity: the volume says a Ge'ez speaker was not necessarily an Aksumite, because a person could be Semitic in origin, Aksumite by nationality and Greek by culture, or Beja or Nubian by birth. Use in the evidence lesson: a language or script is a clue to culture, not a census of people.

Almost no early Aksumite literature survives: there are no parchment manuscripts before the thirteenth century, so the early record is inscriptions and coins (in Sabaean, Ge'ez and Greek, seldom together). Use in the evidence lesson: the medium decides what survives.

Ezana's Nubian war (DAE II, after his conversion): he records killing 602 men and 415 women and children of the Nobatae, justified as punishment for broken oaths, under the Lord of Heaven and Earth. The coins of Lyouel are the first to name Christ. Use in the Ezana lesson as a source that justifies violence in Christian terms.

Kaleb's reign: the traditional account has him abdicate to a monastery after the 525 Arabian war, but another text has him on the throne until 542. The volume says a dating error is possible. Use in the Kaleb lesson with the two dates shown.

The Sahara was not wholly black: a survey by Chamla found that only about one-quarter of the skeletons of the Neolithic and protohistoric period were black, and over 40 per cent showed no negroid features. The 'Ethiopians' of the classical sources were dark-skinned people of mixed type, not a single race. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson, with the figure attributed, before any claim about a black Sahara.

Burial type and status: the volume calls it prejudice to claim that negroid skeletons were slaves, and says the proportion of Garamantes cannot be read off skeletal counts. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson and the evidence lesson: a body's features do not show a person's status without a text.

Classical words for peoples describe colour, not ethnicity: 'Ethiopian' means 'burnt face' or 'man of colour', and the Greek and Roman writers applied it to Saharan and Maghrib peoples. The term is thought to appear on the Pylos tablets. Use in the written-sources lesson as a term to translate with care.

From about 2700 BC the Maghrib was largely cut off from the rest of Africa by the drying Sahara and linked to Iberia, Sicily and Sardinia by sea, leaving the Tripolitanian corridor as the only land route. Use in the Maghrib and trans-Saharan opening lessons.

Agriculture was not brought to North Africa by the Phoenicians. Berbers grew hard wheat, barley, beans and chick-peas and used a wooden-share plough and oxen long before Phoenician arrival, and the tombs with pottery mark the agricultural zones. The Phoenicians' main effect was on tree crops (olive, vine), and even there the Berbers grafted oleaster. Use in the Carthage lesson in place of any Phoenician-introduced-farming claim.

Origin of the Saharan chariot is disputed. The Sea Peoples are said to have taught the Libyans, but the Saharan chariots are sporting vehicles, unlike the Aegean ones; the volume favours Egyptian chariots as the source (Holscher). Use in the trans-Saharan lesson on the horse and the chariot, with both views shown.

A single inscription can merge campaigns: the Karnak text lists Libyans and the Peoples of the Sea together, though they may come from separate campaigns. The volume says that even if the Sea Peoples served with Libyans, their role in Libyan civilisation is overstated. Use in the evidence lesson: a combined text can make two events look like one.

Projecting the past: the volume says it is hazardous to read later pre-Islamic or Roman religious customs back into the protohistoric Libyans, because only funerary rites survive from the earlier period. Use in the evidence lesson on religion: label any pre-Roman religious claim by its source date.

Libyan burial and the cult of the dead: bodies were laid folded, tombs sometimes held a sacrificed horse or a servant, the ancestors were consulted by sleeping on tombs (Nasamonians, Herodotus), and cemeteries grew around revered dead. The volume suggests a sovereign's dead could become the focus of a kingdom's cult. Use in the Numidian kingdom lesson on royal tombs.

The ram was the main cult animal of the Libyans, worshipped as Ammon and spread across the Sahara; Herodotus says they sacrificed only to the sun and moon. The volume says the Theban Ammon may have been becoming the dominant god before Phoenician arrival, but this theory (Leglay) is not fully proven. Use in the Siwa and Ammon part of the Sahara lesson.

Hostile sources for Carthage: no Carthaginian literature survives, and the Greek and Roman writers who describe it were its enemies. Roman towns sit over most Phoenician sites, so archaeology is limited. Use in the written-sources lesson for Carthage as the model case of a source written by the enemy.

Grave goods are not a measure of wealth: the volume notes that fifth-century Carthaginian graves look poor and austere, but that does not mean the community was poorer, since goods in graves are not indicators of wealth or poverty. Use in any lesson that infers wealth from burial.

Outside names are labels: 'Numidae' was derived by the Greeks from a word meaning 'to graze' and called them nomads, but the volume says there was no essential difference between Numidians and Mauri, both largely pastoral. Use in the lesson on Maghrib peoples: give the classical name and say it is a Greek or Roman label.

Carthage's founding date is not secure. Tradition gives 814 BC (Cadiz 1110, Utica 1101, which the volume calls legendary); the earliest firm archaeology is from the middle of the eighth century BC, and permanent settlement on the Maghrib coast began about 800 BC. Use in the Carthage lesson as a range, and say the early settlements were small, a few hundred people.

Tribute and the Libyans: the interior Libyans paid a quarter of their crops in tribute (half during the First Punic War) and supplied soldiers, and Polybius says the Carthaginians rewarded the governors who extracted most. The volume calls this a justified criticism, and the mercenary revolt after the First Punic War drew on it. Use in the Carthage empire lesson.

Hanno's Periplus: the Greek text is said to translate a Carthaginian report, but it gives no purpose, names few places, and the Carthaginians kept trade secret. Pliny says that many Greeks and Romans told fabulous tales from it. Use in the written-sources lesson: a famous voyage account may reveal little and attract invention.

Ancient population figures are guesses: Strabo's figure of 700,000 for Carthage would give an impossible density, and the volume prefers about 400,000 with slaves, as a guess. Use in any city-size claim: name the source, say whether it is a guess, and check the density.

Saharan trade before the Arab period was hard because there were no camels in North Africa. Carthage's trade with the interior left no archaeology, and the only desert goods named are carbuncles, with slaves, ivory and skins suggested. The volume dates the integration of the Sahara into a wider cultural world to the early Arab period. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson, and say the camel is the reason the earlier trade is hard to see.

Carthaginian Atlantic trade: Himilco explored the Atlantic coast of Spain and France towards Brittany to control tin, but no Phoenician object has been found in Britain or Brittany, so tin probably came through local intermediaries. Silver from Spain mattered more than tin. Use in the Atlantic trade opening lesson, with the tin route marked as inferred.

Strabo's claim that Masinissa turned nomads into farmers is an exaggeration; the real change was a large rise in cereal area and export under him, with stock-rearing still dominant. The population of 200,000 given to his capital under his son is called a gross exaggeration. Use in the Numidia lesson, with the claim marked and the cereal rise stated.

Matho's revolt (about 241-237 BC) by 20,000 mercenaries, half of them Libyans, took Utica and Tunis and issued coins inscribed 'Libyon' in Greek, showing the Libyans' own political claim. The volume says the ferocity reflects Carthaginian harshness to the Libyans. Use in the Carthage and Libyan lesson as evidence of Libyan identity under Carthaginian rule.

Battle losses are reported as ancient totals (25,000 soldiers and 70,000 rowers in one Roman storm loss, 10,000 rowers at Mylae), not verified counts. Use with the same caution as the army sizes: say who gives the figure.

Mixed Libyan-Phoenician culture: Phoenician was culturally dominant but a minority; Neo-Punic inscriptions lasted into the second century AD, and the title sufet was used in about thirty towns from Volubilis to Leptis Magna. Use in the Numidia and Maghrib lesson as the evidence for a long-lived mixed culture.

The Libyan script is still not read: it appears on Dougga inscriptions from the second century BC and on Roman stelae, and resembles the script of the modern Tuareg in a way the volume says it cannot explain. Use in the evidence lesson: a script that is not read gives no text, however old it looks.

Mauretania was run by Mauri royal families (Bocchus I, Bocchus II, Bogud II) before Augustus installed Juba II (25 BC) and his son Ptolemy, who was executed in AD 40, so provincialisation came in AD 44. Use in the Mauretania lesson as the stages from kingdom to province.

column4: ch-021.txt chunk 1 (Ch 19 Mahjoubi) vs ch-019.txt chunk 4
column5: Date of the Mauretanian provinces: Warmington (ch-019) says Mauretania became two provinces in AD 44; Mahjoubi (ch-021) says Claudius organised Caesariensis and Tingitana at the end of AD 42. Show both in the Mauretania lesson, or give AD 42-44 as the period, and say which year is in which source.

Tacfarinas's war (eight years under Tiberius) is better read as a land war than a clash of civilisation and nomads. Tacitus gives his demand as the right to land, after conquest had seized the fertile land for veterans, companies and senators. Use in the Roman Africa lesson on why the resistance lasted.

Biased sources on conquest: all the record of Berber resistance comes from Roman literary and inscribed texts with a Roman point of view, and earlier colonial-era historians added their own bias. Use in the written-sources lesson as the case of a conquered people known only through the conquerors.

Roman army size is an estimate: the Legio III Augusta had 5000-6000 men in theory, and the whole African garrison may have been 25,000-30,000 in the second century. The later limitanei were peasant soldiers on fortified farms who introduced irrigation and made the limes a zone of trade and culture. Use in the Roman Africa lesson on the frontier.
Caligula had Ptolemy of Mauretania killed (AD 40), and the volume's view is that Octavian had chosen indirect rule first. Use in the Mauretania lesson as the stage from client kingdom to province.

Roman Africa was run through chiefs as well as cities: tribal chieftains were given subsidies and imperial investiture in return for supplying men to guard the limes, and cities paid the Stipendium or were exempt by charter. Use in the Roman Africa lesson on indirect rule across the frontier.

Colonists were few: the Augustan colonists in Africa are put at no more than 15,000-20,000, which the volume calls 'not a mass-settlement area'. The Roman urban system was large (at least 500 towns in North Africa, 200 in the proconsular province), though how much was inherited from Punic and Numidian times is unclear. Use in the Roman Africa lesson on settlement and cities.

Pliny's list of African towns and their legal status is controversial and hard to read (Pliny gives six colonies, fifteen towns of Roman citizens and thirty free towns for the Augustan period). Use it as an ancient list to be checked, not a settled fact.

Roman Africa's population is disputed by method: Courtois gives about 4 million (2.5 million in towns, from 500 cities at 5,000 each); Charles-Picard gives about 6.5 million at the height of prosperity; Lezine gives 1.3 million town-dwellers for Carthage and Sousse. Use as the worked example of density-based estimates: show the method and the range, never one figure.

Africa as granary: the Roman corn was tribute from a conquered country, and the annona took about one-seventh of output (about 18 million bushels under Nero). A good many peasants lived on millet or barley because the corn left after seed was too little, and drought brought famine. Use in the Roman economy lesson to correct the image of an abundant granary.

Tenancy on imperial estates: the Lex Manciana and Lex Hadriana set the coloni's rent at one-third of crops plus labour days, with a right of use that could be inherited or sold. The Souk el-Khemis inscription (under Commodus) shows the conductores cheating tenants. The volume reads this as the start of the bound peasant of later times. Use in the land and tenancy lesson.

column4: ch-021.txt chunk 4 (Ch 19 Mahjoubi) vs ch-019.txt chunk 2
column5: Camels: Warmington (ch-019) says there were no camels in North Africa before the Arab period, which explains the difficulty of trans-Saharan trade; Mahjoubi (ch-021) says the dromedary was increasingly used from the second and third centuries AD, probably introduced gradually rather than in a sudden influx. Use the timing as the second-to-third century AD in the trans-Saharan lesson, and say the sources differ on when.

Roman contact with the Fezzan: Cornelius Balbus attacked the Garamantes (19 BC) and took Garama and Cidamus. An expedition under Julius Maternus (probably under Domitian) reached Garama and went on to Agisymba, where rhinoceros were reported. Gold came from the placers of Guinea by several caravan routes; Rome sent wine, metalware, pottery, textiles and glass. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson on the Roman side.

Who counted as Roman: the constitutio Antoniniana of 212 gave citizenship to all free inhabitants except the dediticii, who were tribal people outside municipal life, so the tribes beyond the cities stayed outside Roman society. African senators appear from Vespasian's time (about 100 by about 170). Use in the Roman society lesson, with the tribal exclusion stated.

Late Roman social change: under the later empire the decurions were replaced in power by great landowners (principales), while the curiales grew poorer and their offices became hereditary, and the coloni were tied to the land. Seigneurial estates and the lowest-level justice of the landowner appear by the end of the fourth century. Use in the Roman Africa lesson on the decline, and as the bridge to the Vandal and Byzantine periods.

Gods under Roman names: the African Saturn continued Baal Hammon and Juno-Caelestis continued Tanit, so the Punic cult kept its character under Roman names, while Romanisation changed the stelae's signs, temples and language of dedication. Use in the religion lesson on continuity under new names.

Early African Christianity: a synod of 71 bishops at Carthage (about 220) and another of 90 bishops (about 240) show Christian communities across many cities. Christians were executed at Scilli (180) and Perpetua and Felicity died in the Carthage arena (203). Latin, not Greek, was the church's language from the start. Use in the Roman Christianity lesson, with the dates attributed.

Chronology of Roman decline: the volume says the old view of a fourth-century town decline is now to be revised, since there is epigraphy of building and third-century houses. Use in any lesson on urban decline: say the picture has been revised.

Partisan sources and a word with a history: the main Vandal sources (Victor of Vita, Fulgentius, Procopius) are openly hostile, and the English word 'vandalism' was coined only at the end of the eighteenth century, so the image of Vandal destruction is a later judgment. Use in the historiography and written-sources lessons: check who wrote, and when a term was coined.

The Vandal kingdom was not an economic collapse: the volume says the monetary economy, external trade and agriculture show no obvious decline, Africa was called a 'grain empire', and the Lex Manciana was kept. Decay is clearest in some towns. Use in the Vandal lesson: the archaeology corrects the literary image.

Byzantine rule used Berber chiefs as vassals: investiture was granted to Iaudas (Aures), Guenfan, Antalas and Coutzina (High Steppes) and Carcazan (Tripolitania), who ran their own lands with little central control. The volume calls this a continuity of 'Eternal Africa'. Use in the late-antique lesson on Berber polities.

Byzantine strategy was a chain of fortresses (Tebessa, Haidra, Timgad, Sabratha, Kelibia) rather than an advance: the Byzantine frontier never went west of Setif, and the Byzantines had to defend to the heart of the country. The volume compares the late Byzantine strongholds with later Spanish presidios. Use in the Byzantine lesson.

Independent post-Roman rulers are known from rare allusions: Masuna ('king of the Moors and the Romans', early sixth century, Altava and Tlemcen), Masties (Aures, 'dux for sixty-seven years'), Garmul (who beat a Byzantine army in 571), and a Tingitane principality known from Volubilis and the Souk el-Gour mausoleum. Use in the post-Roman lesson as the named rulers and what they left.

Readings of the same inscription differ: Masties' inscription from Arris (Aures) has been argued both ways (Courtois against Carcopino), and the Tenes treasure is read as a wealthy family's jewels by Heurgon but as a thief's haul by the reviewer. Use in the evidence lesson: show both readings of one object and say what each depends on.

Camels in fifth- and sixth-century warfare: the Byzantines fought the Levathae and Louata nomads, who used camels, and had to cut down a ring of animals tied together before they could beat them in the open. The volume uses this to show camels' role in economy and tactics. Use in the Sahara and nomad lesson.

De-Romanisation was not total: the 'Moors and Romans' of Masuna's and Masties' realms were a joint formula, with Latin still used in Tiaret, Altava, Tlemcen and Volubilis into the seventh century. The volume says the trend away from Rome was irreversible but gradual. Use in the post-Roman lesson; avoid 'the Latin disappeared' as a single date.

column4: ch-023.txt chunk 1 (Ch 20 Salama) vs ch-021.txt chunk 4 (Ch 19 Mahjoubi)
column5: Roman reach into the Sahara: Mahjoubi (ch-021) says Balbus subdued Garama and Cidamus (19 BC) and Maternus reached Agisymba. Salama (ch-023) says Balbus's raid covered only the south of the Maghrib and the Fezzan, since the names are ambiguous, and Ptolemy's Niger is a waterway in southern Algeria; Agisymba is left open. Show the claim as disputed, and do not state Roman arrival at the Niger.

column4: ch-023.txt chunk 1 (Ch 20 Salama) vs ch-005.txt chunk 2
column5: Hanno's Periplus: Salama says ancient ships could not have returned from beyond Cape Juby, locates Cerne at Essaouira-Mogador, and calls the text an unskilled plagiarism of Herodotus (Germain). Earlier in the volume the voyage is treated as contested, not as a forgery. Show the range: real voyage to Morocco, weak evidence beyond, forgery argued.

Ptolemy's Geography gives exact coordinates, which made his African interior look well-known. Its names were matched to modern places by sound, and modern work shows it reaches only the south of the Maghrib. Use in the evidence lesson: exact figures give false confidence when the names were matched by sound.

Roman objects reached far into the desert in the third and fourth centuries (Abalessa, Tassili, Ghat, the Tin Hinan group), so the Roman view of the desert improved after the first two centuries, even though the written texts stop before then. Use in the Sahara lesson on archaeology over texts.

Central and northern Saharan people in protohistory were mainly light-skinned, with Tuareg-like features, whose origin is thought to lie north-east of Africa; the modern Haratin are thought to descend from the enslaved sedentary Ethiopians of Herodotus. The volume says blood-group work may settle this. Use in the Sahara peoples lesson as a claim still open.

Evidence rule for routes: one isolated Roman coin proves little, since northern Saharan peoples were still using Roman coins in the nineteenth century. What counts is a pattern of finds that falls on a caravan route known from other sources. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson and any claim that a coin or object shows a route.

Tin Hinan: the Ahaggar tomb at Abalessa (second half of the fourth century AD) is dated by a Roman coin of Constantine (AD 313-324) and by radiocarbon on the bed (about AD 470, plus or minus 130). Her wealth is put down to a position in trans-Saharan trade. Use in the Sahara state and trade lesson, with both dates and their margins.

Roman goods in the Sahara show Garamantic trade, not Roman presence: the objects were spread by Garamantic and neighbouring groups who passed them from one to the next, and a local chief may have taken tolls on passing traders. The Garamantes are a state built on foreign relations, from the late Punic era to the Arab conquest. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson as the middlemen model.

Animals were Rome's main draw from the Sahara: 9,000 beasts were killed at the opening of the Flavian amphitheatre and 11,000 at Trajan's triumph (106), mostly from North Africa, and elephants and rhinoceroses came from further south. Ivory was probably part of the southern trade. Use in the Roman trade lesson on the amphitheatre demand.

No evidence of a Roman trade in black slaves, and gold from the Niger or Guinea reached Rome only by hypothesis; the inventories of gold regions never list Africa. A secret gold trade from Senegal to southern Morocco is possible, and the Arabs had contact with it by 734. Use with the phrase hypothesis in any Roman gold claim.

Dating rock art and script: the Libyan alphabet and Tifinagh show Carthaginian influence (no firm Libyan writing north of the Sahara before the third or second century BC), but Tifinagh changed over time, so Libyco-Berber rock drawings with letters can be misdated, and camels are hard to date. Use in the rock-art lesson: dating by script needs a firm reference.

The camel's arrival, the three-way dating: it reached Egypt in the Persian and Hellenistic periods, Caesar captured 22 camels from Juba I in 46 BC, and camels were in Roman amphitheatre games by the late first century AD. The volume says camels spread slowly over several centuries, and by the fourth century were plentiful in northern Tripolitania (Leptis could be asked for 4,000). Use this range in the trans-Saharan lesson, and correct any earlier claim that camels came only with the Arabs.

Rome's Sahara policy: first destroy the strongest Saharan states (the Nasamones and Garamantes were reduced by the height of the Empire), then hold the line with a network of forts. Camel-mounted nomads (Austuriani, Marmarides, Mazices) returned from the fourth century and wore the limes down. The volume ties the Sahara to Rome's eventual fall. Use in the Roman-Saharan lesson.

Iron came to the Niger region by an open question: carbon-14 dates show iron working in Chad and northern Nigeria in the second and first centuries BC, and its origin is argued as African invention, Mediterranean transfer across the central Sahara, or transfer from Kush by way of Kordofan and Darfur. The volume says the Meroitic route is probable. Use in the iron lesson, marked as open.

Stone tools do not date farming: ground-stone axes appear among hunter-gatherer kits more than 7,000 years ago and were still used in the Zaire basin less than a thousand years ago, and pottery was used by hunters beside farmers. Use in the Neolithic lesson to say that 'Neolithic' is inconsistent in Africa, and to separate tool types from food production.

Radiocarbon has no fixed dates in sub-Saharan Africa: the variability for the period may run over several centuries, so 'early iron age' is set around 1000 BC. The early iron age is defined as persistent iron use, not occasional tools. Use in the chronology lesson: give the spread of the date, not one year.

Bantu origin: three accounts disagree. Greenberg (vocabulary of about 800 languages, 42% shared with nearest West African languages) puts the source in the Nigeria-Cameroon border area; Guthrie (about 350 Bantu languages, 2400 root sets) puts it in the grasslands south of the Zaire forest, with a proto-Bantu who could forge iron and knew boats; Ehret favours a forest source before 1000 BC. Use the Bantu lesson with all three shown and the disagreement stated.

Linguistic evidence is used to read archaeology: the proto-Bantu word for forest meant thicket, and words for fishing with a line, canoe, paddle and forging are common, so the volume concludes the proto-Bantu lived south of true forest and knew iron. Use in the Bantu lesson as an inference from words, not proof.

Agriculture was not simply carried from south-west Asia: earlier views saw African farming as late and diffused from the Nile. Murdock argued for an African source in the Futa Jallon, and the volume says yams, one rice, sorghum and the oil palm were indigenous to West Africa. Use in the agriculture lesson to replace any diffusion-from-Asia claim.

column4: ch-024.txt chunk 2 (Ch 21 Posnansky) vs ch-014.txt chunk 3 (Ch 13 de Contenson)
column5: Meroe and iron: de Contenson (ch-014) says Meroe played the primary role in spreading metal techniques across Africa; Posnansky (ch-024) says the Meroe dispersal theory has the least evidence, iron is rare in Nubia before about 400 BC, and there is no smelting before about 200 BC (Tylecote). Show both in the Meroe and metal lessons, and say the Meroe claim is weak.

Four schools on where iron came from: spread from the Nile (Meroe, the older view), from North Africa via Phoenician or Saharan routes (the Nigerian dates of Taruga, fifth or fourth century BC), an indigenous invention (Diop, and Wai Andah in chapter 24), or Mediterranean links to Mauretania. The volume says West Africa has the earliest dates, so iron probably spread south and east from there. Use in the iron lesson as four schools, none proven.

Iron dates move: iron working in East Africa was dated about AD 1000 in the early 1960s and is now at least 750 years earlier; Ghana's Hani furnace (second century AD) replaced an older date of about AD 900. Use in the iron chronology, with the older dates called superseded. Dates from one site cannot yet set a region's date.

Horse and chariot contact across the Sahara by the middle of the first millennium BC: chariot engravings run from the Tripolitanian coast through Tassili and Hoggar to the middle Nile, and from the Moroccan coast to Mauretania, and the chariot and horse are not native to the Sahara. Use in the Sahara and trans-Saharan lesson for the earliest evidence of contact.

No Carthaginian, Phoenician or Egyptian object dated and confirmed has been found on the West African coast, so the Necho and Hanno voyages had no impact there, even if they happened. Germain's textual work makes the Periplus a late fabrication; Ferguson accepts a voyage to the Gabon estuary. Use with the Hanno lesson: the volume's own view is that the evidence is missing, not that the voyage is proved.

Rock art shows regular routes to the Sudanic belt by about 500 BC, with chariots and carts (1100-400 BC where datable), and horses, bullocks and donkeys on routes; the western route is the stronger for copper and gold. Bovill suggests the three Carthaginian towns of Tripolitania were close together to control the Garamantic road. Carbuncles, emeralds, slaves, civet and ostrich products are the trade goods suggested. Use in the trans-Saharan lesson on routes and goods, with 'suggested' attached to each good.

Words as evidence of trade: the Wolof, Serer and Dyula word for gold (urus) is similar to a Punic word (haras), and the volume suggests traders on the Moroccan coast spread the word south with the gold trade. The chapter says this is a speculation. Use in the lesson on trade terms: a word match is a clue, to be tested against dates.

Western Sudan before Ghana: Senegambian tumuli and megaliths show gold and iron working and Maghribian influence before the rise of Old Ghana, and the wealth of their builders by about AD 1000 is the strongest sign of pre-Islamic trade. Camels may have been used on the western route before the Arab conquest. Use in the Ghana lesson, marked as an inference from tumuli.

Textbook claim corrected: there was no commercial contact, direct or indirect, between East Africa and India before the seventh century AD, and India-Middle East trade before the Periplus was mostly luxuries. The coast was its own world, with trade started by mariners from the northern Indian Ocean rim. Use in the Swahili origins lesson to replace any early India-coast trade claim.

Coins with no site: the East African coin finds (Kimoni, the Zanzibar Museum envelopes, Bur Gao, Dimbani) were found without excavated context. The Bur Gao hoard mixes Ptolemaic, Roman and Byzantine coins with Mamluk and Ottoman ones, so Chittick dates its deposit to the sixteenth century and Wheeler accepts a later addition. Worked example: a mixed hoard is dated by its latest coin, not by its oldest.

Dating the Periplus is disputed: Schoff and Miller put it in the late first century AD, Warmington about AD 60, Pirenne in the early third century, and Mathew in the early second. Ptolemy's Geography (about AD 156) takes its East African material from Marinus of Tyre. Use in the source-review lesson on the Periplus: give the range and name the argument for each date.

Population before trade: the Periplus describes the coast's people as very tall, with fishing and dug-out canoes, but no deep-sea dhows; Oliver ties them to Kushitic highland agriculturalists, and iron-using Bantu speakers moved up the coast in the early centuries AD. The volume says the coast was at a low level of technology before international trade. Use in the Swahili origins lesson with the Kushitic and Bantu claims marked as inference.

Monsoon limits: before the seventh century the dhows' radius was probably as far as Zanzibar, since trade was direct exchange with market-towns; the entrepot at Kilwa for the southern coast came only in the medieval period. Use in the Kilwa lesson as the point where the trade system changed.

Ivory drew the coast in: the Ptolemies set up elephant-hunting posts on the African Red Sea coast to break the Seleucid hold on Indian ivory. Eudoxus made the first direct voyage to India (about the late second century BC) with a pilot who may have been Arab. Arab trade down the East African coast probably began about the second century BC, but no archaeology confirms it. Use in the Swahili origins lesson, stating that the early Arab trade is inferred.

Miller's cinnamon route is not supported: Miller proposed Indonesian voyages to Madagascar and East Africa carrying cinnamon by raft, but the Periplus route follows the northern Indian Ocean rim, and Indonesian migration to Madagascar is now dated to the first millennium AD. Use in the lesson as a bold theory with the textual test that failed.

Rhapta: the Periplus calls it the last known market-town and Ptolemy (about AD 156) calls it a metropolis, with no Arab overlord named. The volume says this may mean the trade had enough wealth to end Arab suzerainty. Its site is disputed: the Pangani valley (Baxter and Allen) or between Pangani and Dar es Salaam (Datoo), with the Rufiji less likely. Use in the Swahili origins lesson, as the debate and the negative evidence.

Mixed-parentage agents: the Periplus says Muza's Arab captains and agents married into coastal families, knew the language and the coast, and acted for the Himyar trade. The volume suggests this may begin a class of coastal traders of mixed parentage. Use in the Swahili origins lesson as the earliest hint of the Swahili mixed society.
