Gonja in the Pare hills has sea-shells and shell beads that show coastal links, but the evidence cannot be dated earlier than about AD 500. Use in the Swahili interior lesson with that date as the earliest firm link.

Testing a coin series: the Haywood collection has six mid-second-century Roman coins, then a gap, then 79 coins from the late third and fourth centuries; the Dimbani collection has one first-century coin and the rest third and fourth century. The volume reads the gap as possible direct trade ending, with a brief revival around AD 300. Use in the coin-evidence lesson: show the gap, and say why the samples are too small to prove a stop.

Indian demand for ivory: from about AD 500 India needed ivory for bridal ornaments that were destroyed at each death or divorce, and by the tenth century India and China were the main markets for East African ivory. The Indian market served East Africa until the nineteenth century. Use in the Swahili city-state and ivory lesson as the second phase of trade.

Adulis rose as the ivory port: as the Roman market shrank, upper-Nile ivory went through Adulis to Persia and India, and Ethiopia took some of the Arabs' middleman trade. Use in the Aksum lesson on Aksum's trade and the Red Sea, linking it with the Himyar decline.

Persia and the Shirazi tradition: Persian ships dominated the Indian Ocean in the sixth and seventh centuries, and the Shirazi migration tradition may begin here. The only pre-Islamic coastal finds are five Parthian and Sassanid coins, so the tradition is unproved. Use in the Swahili origins lesson with the Shirazi story marked as a tradition.

Dependence and the coastal class: the volume says the coast's racially mixed trading class grew rich from international trade and so could not easily leave it, and that the slave export drained people from the coast. Use in the Swahili society lesson with the dependence reading stated as one reading.

Hunter-gatherers before the Bantu: rock-shelter paintings and Wilton-type stone tools link central Tanzania (Hadza, Sandawe) with southern Africa, so the savannah hunter tradition once covered much of eastern and southern Africa. Use in the pre-Bantu lesson on the people who were there first, with the Hadza and Sandawe as surviving evidence.

Legend versus archaeology: Kikuyu stories of the Gumba forest people are vague and reworked by informants, but archaeology shows high-forest settlers with circular ridge depressions and pottery in the last two thousand years. The volume says there is no good ground to call them pygmies. Use in the lesson as the case where legend and dig agree on a people but not on their identity.

Pygmies in East Africa are not proved: the historical references to pygmies in East Africa are mostly ethnographic misconceptions, folklore, or San-type hunters, and the Lupemban-Tshitolian forest remains stop east of Rwanda. Use in the East Africa lesson: say that pygmy presence in East Africa is unproved.

Kansyore pottery at Lake Victoria (first millennium BC) has affinities with much older dotted wavy-line wares, so the aquatic tradition may run back for millennia, with only its last phase found. Forest clearance around the lake suggests a new land use. Use in the Lake Victoria lesson on the pre-Bantu fishers.

Classification is a tool: the volume follows the language-based scheme of Ogot and Kiernan and says that language groups are the clearest way for historians to classify peoples, though language does not fix identity. Use in the East Africa lesson: say the grouping is linguistic, and use it as a convention, not an identity.

First East African cattle: long-horned, humpless cattle reached the Kenya highlands and Rift valley about three thousand years ago, and the first pastoralists left stone-bowl culture: grindstones, milk vessels, cairn burials. Their economy was not only herding, and some cultivation is likely. Use in the first-pastoralist lesson with the cultivation point marked as probable.

A discredited theory can have some true facts: the volume says the Hamitic theory of a tall, light-skinned pastoral invasion was built on racist assumptions and an obsession with origins, but some of its observations were sound. Its error was to pick one external influence (the Kushitic and pastoral element) and treat it as the whole story. Use in the historiography lesson: separate the frame of a theory from its facts.

Bantu expansion as settlement, not conquest: the volume calls it vast and fast colonisation of empty lands by farmers with iron and seed, not a military campaign or slow stages. The northern Bantu line was drawn about 1500 years ago, and about one-third of East Africa stayed non-Bantu. Brick-built iron furnaces in Rwanda and Kivu mark a productive industry. Use in the Bantu lesson: say the expansion was rapid and colonising, with the non-Bantu zones named.

Crops and dates: bananas came from south-east Asia and probably reached East Africa only in the first millennium AD, after the great Bantu expansion, and maize and cassava arrived very recently. Use in any lesson on Bantu crops: name the sorghum and millet staples and do not date bananas to the expansion.

What survives: early Bantu sites are identified mainly by pottery, not iron, because iron tools were too valuable to throw away and corroded when lost. Use in the evidence lesson: the commonest find is the least valued object, so a site's identity may rest on a sherd.

Bantu pottery and identity: the dimple-based (Urewa) wares around Lake Victoria and westwards look like a conscious Bantu style, while Kwale ware in north-east Tanzania and Kenya needed Bantu marks because other peoples there already made pottery. The volume puts the Bantu nucleus west of Lake Victoria near the forest edge. Use in the Bantu lesson with the pottery signature stated.

Early Bantu trade was small: the earliest sites have no coastal or foreign objects, and the trade in bars of iron and pots is inferred only for about 1500 years ago. Salt came from reeds and brine, and the only early exploited source is the Uvinza brine springs in western Tanzania. Use in the early Bantu trade lesson: trade was local and light before about AD 1000.

Highland Nilotes: they took the Rift valley over the first millennium AD, adopting cattle and grain while learning from the Kushites, and their age-sets, circumcision and fish taboo mix Kushitic and Nilotic origins. Their ironworking probably came from the north, separate from the Bantu. Use in the Nilotes lesson, with the iron source stated as probable.

A loaded word and misread evidence: 'megalithic' serves no historical purpose in East Africa. The Azanian civilisation (Huntingford) and Murdock's megalithic Kushites rested on a single people for every feature. Cairns date to the late stone age (two to three thousand years ago), rock-cut wells may be early pastoral, and so-called ancient roads are often cattle tracks. Use in the lesson on the megalithic claim as a worked example of evidence misread.

Engaruka is not a city: the stone-lined irrigation furrows and terraced fields (about 20 square kilometres) belonged to a concentrated peasant community, dated to the second millennium AD (a first-millennium date was an unrepresentative radiocarbon result). The city of 30,000 in older books is wrong. Use in any lesson on Engaruka and on the megalithic claim.

Sirikwa Holes: the many sunken enclosures in the western Kenya highlands were defended kraals of the Kalenjin, with houses of wood and thatch, not pit-dwellings. Stone was used only where the ground had stone, which the volume uses to show that stonework follows the environment as well as culture. Use in the Kenya highlands lesson.

column4: ch-028.txt chunk 1 (Ch 25 Vannoten; West Africa end of ch-027) vs ch-024.txt chunk 3 (Ch 21 Posnansky)
column5: Origin of West African long-distance trade: Posnansky says the search for its origins must begin in the Sahara. The West African section here argues that an internal network (fish, salt, kola, stone axes, pottery, clay from distant sources) came first, from the early iron age, and made trans-Saharan trade possible. Show both and say the internal-first view has the evidence of local traded materials.

column4: ch-028.txt chunk 1 (West Africa end of ch-027)
column5: Ghana's roots: the internal trade network in local goods (Kintampo stone rasps of about 1500 BC in dolomitic marl found in Accra and northern Ghana, and Rim near Ouahigouya, a major axe factory) shows that goods travelled hundreds of miles before Ghana. Use in the Ghana lesson as the internal basis of the trade that Ghana later controlled.

column4: ch-028.txt chunk 1 (West Africa end of ch-027)
column5: Named industries and dating: the 'Uelian Neolithic' of polished hematite axes, first named from surface finds, was found at Buru to be partly iron age, its workshop dated to the seventeenth century. The 'Ubangian' site at Batalimo gave a thermoluminescence date of about AD 380. Use in the Central Africa lesson: a label from surface finds can be wrong on its date.

Language is not people: the volume says the word Bantu is a linguistic term that should not be used for an archaeological iron age or an ethnic group. Use in any lesson on the Bantu: keep language, ethnicity and archaeology as three separate claims.

column4: ch-028.txt chunk 1 (West Africa end of ch-027)
column5: Iron in West Africa did not follow the Near-East stages: sub-Saharan centres seem to go straight from stone to iron with little copper or bronze, and the volume says diffusion theories are not supported by the dates, which may show Nok ironworking near 1000 BC. Use in the iron lesson: do not assume the Mediterranean sequence of copper, bronze, then iron applies in Africa.

Radiocarbon needs a formal link: at Kinshasa, a date of about 270 BC from wood ash with one atypical shard is viewed cautiously because the ash is not formally tied to the shard, and at Sanga two dates (about AD 710 and 880) may not date the same thing, as one came from an unusual grave and the other from a grave with no diagnostic goods, with bones added to a sample. Use in the dating lesson: say what the sample was and what it is tied to.

Iron-age vocabulary is ambiguous: proto-Bantu forging words (forge, hammer, bellows) may be inherited, borrowed, or a shift in meaning (forge from beat), and some metal words are shared with non-Bantu languages. Use in the Bantu iron lesson: a word for iron does not prove the word came with the iron.

Urewe pottery dates: most dates for dimple-based Urewe ware fall between about AD 250 and 400, but one site at Katuruka gives earlier dates, which is hard to assess. The volume says Urewe is homogeneous, with differences that may be local variants and not stages. Use in the early iron age lesson with the spread of dates stated.

Sanga and Katoto (upper Lualaba, roughly seventh to ninth centuries AD): Sanga has 175 graves opened, rich copper and iron goods, and a minority with copper crosses that may have brought copper 180 miles from the south. Katoto has multiple burials, a smith's grave with sacrificed women and children, and glass and shell beads from both oceans. Use in the Central Africa lesson on the wealthy iron-working societies, with dates stated as broad.

Two large neighbouring cemeteries that barely interacted: the volume says it is astonishing that Sanga and Katoto, close together and apparently contemporary, had almost no contact, and that the size of the cemeteries points to large populations on the upper Lualaba by the end of the first millennium AD. Use in the lesson as an open question.

The iron-Bantu link is open: iron slag at Katuruka dates to about 500-400 BC in radiocarbon years (calibrated dates are older), and the volume suggests Bantu-speakers may have learned iron during the expansion rather than bringing it. Use in the Bantu lesson: state that the link between Bantu and iron is an open question with the new dates shown, and the old one labelled as now questioned.

Method under question: the volume says glottochronology (dating languages by their rate of change) is itself questioned, and that the old chain from Guthrie's linguistics to archaeology to an evolutionary idea of a Fertile Crescent origin chimed too neatly. Use in the Bantu lesson: name the method behind each date.

Pottery is not diagnostic: most pottery in Central Africa cannot be told apart as iron age from earlier pottery, so only a few types (Urewe, Kalambo, Chondwe, Kapwirimbwe, Kalundu, Dambwa) count as iron age. Use in any lesson on identifying the iron age from pots.

Economy of early iron age Central Africa: the societies were largely self-sufficient, with agriculture and herding, but hunting and fishing still mattered, and trade was regional in metals, pottery, dried fish and salt, and long-distance in cowries, conus shells and glass beads from the east coast. Trade seems to have been near the big rivers and the lake region. Use in the Central Africa lesson on economy and trade.

Iron-using farmers reached south of the Limpopo by the fourth or fifth century AD (Transvaal, Swaziland), while the earliest iron working in Natal is later, about AD 1050. Hunters were displaced, surviving only in rugged places such as the Drakensberg. Use in the southern Africa lesson on the first farmers, with the Natal date stated as later.

The San diet was mostly plant food: travellers from the 1650s to the 1820s agree that corms of iris-family plants (the 'uyntjes') were the staple, with insects and honey. Game was 'occasionally taken'. Use in the San lesson to correct the image of a hunter-first people. The volume notes that archaeology overstates hunting because bone survives and plant food rarely does.

Archaeology's bias: durable residues (bones, shells, stone) survive, while tubers, corms and plant food rarely do, so the record favours hunting. Only dry shelters preserve plant remains, so the food picture comes from a few sites plus travellers' accounts. Use in the evidence lesson: a diet reconstructed from surviving remains is shaped by what survives.

Colonial labels: 'Hottentot' and 'Bushman' were colonial names, and 'Khoisan' fuses Khoikhoi herders and San hunters, groups the volume says spoke related languages and shared technology but were distinguished by way of life. Use in the southern Africa lesson: name the groups as the colonists did, then say what each term joins or divides.

Ethnographic models: the Kung and G/wi of the Kalahari are used to read extinct groups, as a general model, not a copy. The volume says the model is useful for technology and social organisation and warns about applying it to the past. Use in the southern Africa lesson and any San analogy.

San groups were small: most rarely exceeded twenty people, and the late eighteenth-century groups of 150 and 500 that travellers describe were gathered to defend against colonial raiding parties. Use in the San social-organisation lesson: say the large gatherings were unusual and defensive.

Work and season: rock art and travellers show women with digging-sticks and men with bows, with the women's daily plant gathering the steady food. The corm supply shrank after flowering, and the Cape reckoned time in months before or after 'uyntjes tyd' (onion time), so the seasonal cycle was part of the language. Use in the San economy lesson on the gendered division of labour and seasonal food.

Oxygen isotopes can give seasons: Shackleton measured oxygen-isotope ratios in shells from Nelson Bay Cave and matched them to modern sea temperatures, concluding that the middens built up only in winter. Use in the evidence lesson as a method that dates the season of an activity, not just the date of a deposit.

Coastal and inland contrast: at inland De Hangen, tortoises and dassies dominate, while at coastal Elands Bay Cave they are rare, because coastal people had fish, crayfish and seabirds. Seasonal coastal shellfish filled the winter and spring shortage of corms and fruit. Use in the San settlement-pattern lesson on coast and inland use.

Diffusion argument: pottery could have been invented independently, but domestic animals could not, so when sheep and pottery appear together at the same sites it is taken as diffusion from outside. The volume defends this with local sequences of dates, which iron out sampling problems. Use in the herders lesson as the reasoning behind an inferred spread, stated with its assumptions.

Pottery and sheep reached the southern Cape early: sherds and domestic stock appear together at sites from Angola to the southern Cape between about 2000 and 1600 BC, before the iron age farther north by two to three centuries, and the coastal plain shows the pattern most clearly. Use in the southern Africa lesson on the first herders, with the dates marked as the earliest good associations.

The origin of the Khoi herders is open: the volume favours an East African origin through pottery types, click languages (Hatsa, Sandawe) and sheep, and suggests a westward route through Namibia and the northern Cape. It says these links may be dubious. Use in the herders lesson as an argued hypothesis, not a settled origin.

A pot does not name its maker: the early European accounts that credit pottery to the Khoi are vague, and the volume says some remarks may refer to Cape Khoi in the late seventeenth century, while San pottery is not described at all. Use in the evidence lesson: a pot's attribution rests on the writer's source.

Khoi life and diet: herders ate milk and vegetable staples, and killed stock only for feasts, so their diet overlapped the San's but had milk. Their technology overlapped the San's too, except for rush houses, pottery and metalwork. Namaqua made copper beads and discs in the seventeenth century. Use in the Khoi lesson on diet and technology.

Khoi villages were large: Paterson counted villages of six to nineteen huts, Le Vaillant a Gonaqua horde of about 400 persons in 40 huts, and Dapper a Cochoqua group of 400-450 huts with about 100,000 cattle and 200,000 sheep. Dapper's and Le Vaillant's figures are travellers' estimates, not counts. Use in the Khoi lesson with each figure attributed and the estimate status stated.

San and Khoi: Elphick's sequence for absorbing San into herding societies runs through warfare, clientship, intermarriage and assimilation. The 'Sonqua' served as messengers and mercenaries for Khoi groups, while the Obiqua stole stock. Use in the San-Khoi relations lesson as the mechanism of change, marked as Elphick's argument.

Khoi land management: Sparrman saw Khoi herders burning the veld to renew grass and tuber plants, a practice that the early colonists found was already there when they arrived. Use in any lesson on how herders shaped the land: the burning predates colonists and counts as management.

The early iron age came as a package: food production, metallurgy, pottery and daga-walled villages appear together in southern Africa from the first centuries AD, with no local ancestor for the pottery or the metal, so the volume argues a substantial, rapid movement of population. Use in the southern Africa iron-age lesson as the migration case, with the alternative of local development stated.

Date units: every date in this chapter is in uncorrected radiocarbon years, and the chapter says so. Use in the chronology lesson: when a source gives an uncorrected radiocarbon date, say so, since calendar years differ.

Method order: archaeology is treated as the base for the pre-literate iron age, with historical linguistics as secondary comparison, because oral tradition does not reach this period. Use in any lesson where a linguistic reconstruction is offered for the early iron age: label it secondary.

Zambian early iron-age sequence: the Chondwe group (Copperbelt) has dates from the sixth to the eleventh centuries AD; the Kapwirimbwe site east of Lusaka was occupied from about the fifth century with iron smelting furnaces and no copper; copper appears only in the last phase at Twickenham Road. Kalundu, on the Batoka plateau, has cowrie shells but no glass beads and was displaced by the Kalomo tradition about the mid-ninth century. Use in the Zambia lesson with the dates as uncorrected radiocarbon years.

Copper was scarce in the early iron age: most sites in Zambia and Zimbabwe show iron without copper, and copper came by trade from the Kafue Hook and Wankie sources. Copper bangles and trade-bars at Dambwa-group sites show that trade began early. Use in the metals lesson: iron was local, copper was traded.

Gold and the Indian Ocean: more than a thousand prehistoric gold mines are recorded in Zimbabwe and the bordering Botswana and Transvaal, most since destroyed by mining (the true number was several times higher). Ziwa pottery (late first millennium) found with imported glass beads at gold and copper workings shows the links to the Indian Ocean trade. Use in the Zimbabwe gold lesson before Great Zimbabwe, with the mine count given as a minimum.

Cattle arrived late: sheep and goats came first; cattle appear in Zimbabwe only about the eighth century, and in early iron-age southern Zambia are scarce. Fat-tailed sheep are painted in Zimbabwe rock art, and cattle never. The shift to herding came in the second half of the first millennium (Kalundu, with fewer iron hoes at Victoria Falls). Use in the herding and cattle lesson.

Copper was a luxury and a trade metal: in early iron age times copper was used for small beads and bangles and traded as bars (Kumadzulo has a bar), and people came from far away to the Copperbelt's Roan Antelope sites, judged from the mixed pottery. Large-scale copper mining is a later iron age phenomenon. Use in the metals lesson on copper as a trade good.

Smelting and taboo: early iron-age villages smelted iron inside the settlement, which the volume reads as the absence of the later taboo keeping smelting away from women. The use of tewels (tuyère-like nozzles) does not prove bellows, since natural-draught furnaces also used them. Use in the iron technology lesson, and mark both points as inference from the site.

Zimbabwe's early iron-age groups: Gokomere (fifth to seventh century), Ziwa (most of the first millennium, with copper and glass later), Zhiso (ninth to twelfth century). The Mandau and Madiliyangwa sites show early pottery in the Matopos before Zhiso. Use in the Zimbabwe lesson to set the pottery sequence before Great Zimbabwe.

Start of Zimbabwean gold: the four gold mines with early iron-age pottery date to about the ninth to eleventh century, and the first radiocarbon dates for ancient mines are about the twelfth century. The first Arabic record of Zimbabwean gold bought on the East African coast is in a tenth-century context (al-Mas'udi). The volume finds no convincing evidence of exploitation before the ninth century. Use in the Great Zimbabwe gold lesson, with these dates as ranges.

Summers' India origin for Zimbabwean gold techniques is unconvincing on present evidence; the glass beads and the start of mining are synchronous, so an outside stimulus is possible without an Indian source. Use in the gold lesson: name the proposed sources and say which evidence each rests on.

Ingombe Illede: the gold-bearing burials at Ingombe Illede (near Kariba) are now known not to belong to its late first-millennium occupation, so they cannot be used as early gold evidence. Use in any lesson on the Zambezi gold trade: remove that site from the early-gold list.

Early stone building in Zimbabwe was small-scale: terrace and field walls and simple enclosures from Gokomere, Ziwa and Zhiso, with the most elaborate early form at Maxton Farm (a diorite-block wall with upright monoliths). The stone sequence at Great Zimbabwe itself is later iron age. Use in the Great Zimbabwe lesson: the stone tradition begins in the early iron age, but the great walls come later.

Blank maps reflect research: the chapter says the whole of Mozambique is a blank on its distribution maps and much of Angola and South Africa is poorly investigated, so the history of those areas is unknown rather than absent. Use in any lesson on a map of archaeological sites: the empty region shows where digging has not happened.

Madagascar's settlement date: Indonesians and Africans reached the island between about the fifth and eighth centuries AD, and no later than the ninth. The first Indonesian migration is dated from about the fifth century, with later Neo-Indonesian arrivals (ancestors of the Merina) in later waves. The coastal societies have many features shared with Bantu-speaking Africa. Use in the Madagascar lesson with the date range stated.

Matching names does not prove a loan: the banana has an Indonesian name (fontsy) on the west coast and a Bantu name (akondro) in the central highlands, so either origin can be argued. Haudricourt notes that immigrants gave Indonesian names to native plants that looked like home species. Use in the evidence lesson: a shared name shows a link of some sort, not which direction the plant moved.

Menuthias in Ptolemy and the Periplus is more likely Pemba, Zanzibar or Mafia than Madagascar, since the Periplus route stops there before Rhapta. The Periplus has no sign of Madagascar trade, and the island was probably uninhabited at the time. Use in the Madagascar and Swahili lessons: reject the claim that Greeks or Arabs knew Madagascar under that name.

Names as proof of migrants: Flacourt's Jewish origin (biblical names, circumcision, a Saturday taboo) and Briant's Hebrew comparisons were argued from word matches, while Ferrand gave the Saturday taboo as local fady (taboo) and the Semitic names as Islamic conversion. Use in any lesson on claimed foreign migrations: check whether a custom or word is distinctive or common.

The Waqwaq raids: a tenth-century Persian text (Buzurg ibn Shahriyar) says the Waqwaq attacked Qanbaloh, probably Pemba, about AD 945-6, and then took towns in Sofala; the raiders came from islands six days' sail away, possibly Indonesians via Madagascar. Use in the Swahili and Pemba lessons, with the source and date given and the raiders' origin marked as argued.

The identity of the Waqwaq is open: Faubleé and Mauny read the same text differently, and the volume suggests the raiders were probably negroid with some Indonesians already in the mixed Proto-Malagasy group. Use in the lesson: say the raiders are not identified, and name the two readings.

Indonesian sea traffic to the African coast: Idrisi (twelfth century) says the Zanj had no ships, but traders from Oman and islanders from Sumatra came to trade in Zanj and understood each other's language. The Indonesian presence on the African coast is thought to be small and localised, with no settlement found. Use in the Swahili trade lesson on the twelfth-century links.

The Comoros: the Sima midden at Anjouan (an earth layer under a fifteenth-century mosque, with red-ochre pottery and shells) gives a radiocarbon date of 1550 plus or minus 70 years, the first pre-Islamic evidence there. Ouani cooking pots resemble Malagasy utensils. Use in the Comoros lesson on pre-Islamic settlement, with the one dated site stated.

Glottochronology gives a wide range: comparisons of Malagasy with Malay and within Malagasy dialects allow dates from a little before to well into the first millennium AD, so the method gives no precise date. Use in the Madagascar lesson: state glottochronology's range and rely more on sea-route history.

A tool may not be what it looks like: two adze-like stones from Madagascar could be gunflints worked in the firearms period, and Grandidier's stones from Lamboara were also near the arrival of guns. The volume says no conclusion can be drawn until a stone date is tied to a context. Use in the early-Madagascar lesson: a stone object needs context before its date is used.

Komr and Madagascar: Arabic writers call the island Komr (sometimes with the Comoros), and fifteenth-century charts by Ibn Majid and Suleyman el Mahri show it. A tradition given by Ibn el Mudjawir says Komr people took Aden in one monsoon, and their ship reached Aden by mistake in AD 1228. The volume suggests Islamic trade ended the Indonesian voyages west. Use in the lesson on the end of Indonesian contact, with the Komr name explained.

Bantu speakers reached Madagascar from about the ninth century: Malagasy keeps many Bantu words in all dialects, and Dahl's change from consonant-final to vowel-final structure is explained by a Bantu substratum. The Comoros (Anjouan's language links to Pokomo on the Tana mouth) may have been a stop. Use in the Madagascar and Swahili migration lesson, with the Bantu settlement dated from about AD 900 and the substratum as the argued cause.

A sound change as evidence: the volume argues from one phonetic change (loss of final consonants) to a Bantu substratum, reasoning that speakers of a language without final consonants find another language's finals hard. It is a strong inference, not a proof. Use in the evidence lesson: a structural change can be evidence of contact, and it should be labelled as an inference from linguistics.

Pygmies in Madagascar rejected: the volume says the idea defies geology and navigation, since the island has been isolated since the Tertiary, and pygmies were not sailors. Use in any Madagascar lesson on earliest inhabitants.

Muslims as catalysts: coastal Madagascar shares the myth of Mojomby, the lost island of righteous Muslim traders, and the volume reads Islam as a catalyst that linked Africans who had migrated there, not a culture laid over them. Use in the Madagascar and Islam lesson.

Igbo-Ukwu date: Shaw dates the Igbo-Ukwu copper and bronze to the ninth century AD and argues trade was large by then; many scholars (Lawal, Posnansky) put it well within the second millennium. The volume says the early date needs a large trade and the later date needs a different explanation. Show both dates in the Igbo-Ukwu lesson, and say the ninth-century date is disputed.

Copper in West Africa before AD 1000 is scarce except in Senegal and Mauretania. The Niger-valley tumuli at El Ouladji and Killi (near Segu) hold copper of the late first millennium, but most of their objects were lost early in the twentieth century, so they survive only as illustrations. Use in the copper and Niger lesson, with the lost-objects problem stated.

Salt for the trans-Saharan trade: Taghaza and Awlil were salt sources in the Sahara, in Arabic texts of the late first millennium AD, and possibly older with the Tichitt settlements. Uvinza, Kibiro and Basanga show early salt-making in East and Central Africa by evaporation and boiling. Use in the Sahara salt lesson, with the early east African salt sites marked.

Salt-making is hard to identify: perforated colander pots found on iron-age sites could be used for salt-making or for other food preparation, so a salt-making claim needs more than the vessel. Use in the salt lesson: the vessel alone does not prove the activity.

Laterite and the Senegambian megaliths: the upright laterite blocks of the Senegambian megaliths show that ironworking in the area during the first millennium AD and the use of laterite as ritual stone came together, and the volume suggests smelting the laterite may have led to quarrying it for building. Use in the Senegambia lesson as a suggested link between stone and iron.

Early states, two models: the diffusionist view (Frazer, Baumann, Oliver) says divine kingship spread from Egypt, possibly by way of rainmaking, and that horse-riding iron-using warriors spread the state. The internal view says the similarities of African states may be later accretions, and that states came from trade, scarce minerals, or Carneiro's competition for scarce land. Use in the Ghana and Mali lessons: name both models, and say the diffusion view needs proof.

Population before AD 1000: the volume estimates under 10 million for sub-Saharan Africa, with densities of a handful per square kilometre, villages of one or more lineages, and largely matrilineal societies on the evidence of later oral traditions. Settlement was densest in savannah woodland and dry forest, and the Niger inland delta had many sites. Use in the population lesson, with the estimate and its method stated.

Trade-wind beads and Igbo-Ukwu: more than 150,000 small cane beads, of the Indian Ocean trade-wind type, came from Igbo-Ukwu. If the early date holds, bead trade across the Sahara existed by the late first millennium AD, but the beads' factory cannot be fixed without analysis. Use in the Igbo-Ukwu lesson, with the bead count and the date dispute both stated.

Sanga's wealth and currency: Bisson argues that the eighth- or ninth-century wealth at Sanga came before long-distance trade, since imports are few, and that copper crosses served as currency, so the rulers' prestige came from metal control and craftsmen. Use in the Sanga and Shaba lesson as the internal-wealth reading.

Diffusion is itself a theory to test: the volume says most African scholars see diffusionist views as a way of bringing in outside cultural elements without checking for independent development, and the author agrees. Use in the historiography lesson: diffusion is an argument with its own burden of proof.

Ghana as the only convincing early kingdom: Ghana existed by about AD 700 and may have been emerging for up to a thousand years, with its growth tied to control of copper, iron, gold and salt and to an early agricultural base (Tichitt). The Senegambian megaliths and the Senegal tumuli are seen as contemporary parts of one economic growth. Use in the Ghana lesson: give the AD 700 date as the earliest firm mention and the start as uncertain.

The Meroitic script is still undeciphered, though about 900 documents survive; the volume calls its decipherment the next step, since it would give a classical African language beside Egyptian. Use in the Meroe lesson as the gap that limits what Kush can say about itself.

Meroitic influence on Aksum: the volume dates it to the second and third centuries AD, when Meroitic and Egyptian-Meroitic religion (ankh stele, Hathor, Ptah, Horus, scarabs) shaped Aksumite beliefs before Christianity. Use in the Aksum lesson on the religious links to Meroe.

The conclusion is an editor's frame: it calls Egyptian writing the longest-lived language, says the African history cleavage at AD 1500 is a dogma of historians, and claims a cultural unity across the continent. These are the editors' views, not findings. Use in the lessons: mark the conclusion's claims as the volume's position and test them against the chapters.

Nubian rule of Egypt: the fifty-year Nubian domination (the first part of the 25th Dynasty) joined Egypt and Nubia under Napata, and the Napatan monarchy began after Egypt's power waned in the early first millennium BC. Use in the Kush lesson on the Napatan period as the peak of Kushite power in Egypt.
